                   MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF THE
                        INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS

           Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”),1 the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners

(collectively, the “PJM TOs”) respectfully move for leave to submit this answer in response to the

Response in Opposition and Answer of the Maryland Office of People’s Counsel (“MDOPC”)

filed on September 11, 2026 (“MDOPC Answer”)2 regarding the MDOPC’s complaint initiating


1
    18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213.
2
  For the purpose of this filing, the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners are: American Electric Power Service
Corporation on behalf of its affiliates Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, Kentucky
Power Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling Power Company, AEP Appalachian
Transmission Company, Inc.; The Dayton Power and Light Company d/b/a AES Ohio; Dominion Energy Services,
Inc. on behalf of Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a Dominion Energy Virginia; Duke Energy Business
Services, LLC for Duke Energy Kentucky, Inc. and Duke Energy Ohio, Inc.; Duquesne Light Company; East
Kentucky Power Cooperative; Exelon Corporation on behalf of its affiliates Atlantic City Electric Company,
Baltimore Gas and Electric Company, Commonwealth Edison Company, Commonwealth Edison Company of
Indiana, Inc., Delmarva Power & Light Company, PECO Energy Company, and Potomac Electric Power Company;
FirstEnergy Service Company, on behalf of its affiliates American Transmission Systems, Incorporated, Jersey Central
Power & Light Company, Mid-Atlantic Interstate Transmission LLC, The Potomac Edison Company, Monongahela
Power Company, Keystone Appalachian Transmission Company, and Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line Company
 this proceeding (the “Complaint”). Nothing in the MDOPC Answer demonstrates that MDOPC

has satisfied its burden under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act to show that PJM’s existing

cost allocation methodology is unjust and unreasonable. Nor does the MDOPC Answer establish

why the Complaint should proceed in light of the Commission’s June 18, 2026, order on large load

integration (“Large Load Order”),3 or propose a just and reasonable replacement rate. Thus, as

discussed herein and for the reasons stated in the PJM TOs’ Motion to Dismiss and Answer of July

27, 2026 (“Motion to Dismiss”), the Commission should dismiss or otherwise deny the Complaint.

I.         MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

            The Commission permits answers for good cause shown,4 including where the answer

clarifies issues in dispute or otherwise assists the decision-making process.5 Good cause exists to

accept this answer because it clarifies issues in dispute by addressing new arguments raised by the

MDOPC Answer and corrects MDOPC’s mischaracterization of the PJM TOs’ response to the

Complaint. Specifically, this Answer rebuts MDOPC’s attempt to argue that the Large Load Order

has not superseded its Complaint. Additionally, this Answer demonstrates the flaws in MDOPC’s

justification of its proposed replacement rate and corrects the MDOPC’s contention that the PJM

TOs, guided by “perverse incentives,” are merely defending the status quo.

II.        ANSWER

           With this Answer, the PJM TOs respond to three limited issues raised in the MDOPC

Answer. First, the MDOPC Answer fails to show why the intervening Large Load Order has not



(collectively, the “FirstEnergy Companies”); PPL Electric Utilities Corporation; Public Service Electric and Gas
Company; Rockland Electric Company; and UGI Utilities, Inc.

 rendered its Complaint moot.6 Second, the PJM TOs show how MDOPC’s defense of its flawed

replacement rate confirms the flaws identified in the Motion to Dismiss. Third, the PJM TOs

correct MDOPC’s mischaracterization of the PJM TOs’ motives with respect to the existing cost

allocation methodology. In sum, the MDOPC Answer does not cure the defects in the Complaint,

and the Commission has ample grounds and should dismiss or otherwise deny the Complaint.

           A.           MDOPC Fails to Justify the Complaint Following the Commission’s Large
                        Load Order.

           The Commission’s Large Load Order moots the Complaint because it establishes principles

that will govern a just and reasonable replacement rate.7 MDOPC argues that the issues in the

Complaint and the Large Load Order are distinguishable because the Commission declared its

intent not to “alter or call into question existing regional cost allocation methods for Network

Upgrades.”8 That argument misses the mark. The Large Load Order identifies specific concerns

and makes preliminary findings, including those about mitigating the risk of cost shifting from

large-load growth (the precise harm MDOPC alleges) by proposing tariff changes to improve

transparency and provide for a pro forma cost-recovery agreement ensuring large loads bear a

minimum contribution to the transmission revenue requirement.9

           In addition, the MDOPC’s Answer on mootness is inconsistent with its position in the

Complaint. MDOPC argues that the Complaint is not “subsumed” by the Large Load Order while

conceding that “several issues . . . may be advanced” in that proceeding.10 MDOPC insists that

 regional cost allocation must be treated separately from the issues the Commission is addressing

in the Large Load Order. Yet, it simultaneously argues that the cost-allocation issues require a

coordinated and consistent review of both regional baseline and supplemental projects, and that

addressing both together is necessary to avoid gaming.11 MDOPC cannot demand coordinated,

region-wide treatment of project cost recovery while insisting that the cost allocation methodology

for regional transmission projects be litigated in isolation. Further, MDOPC warns that addressing

supplemental projects alone, without regional baseline projects, would invite gaming and perverse

incentives.12      But carving the RTEP cost allocation methodology from an industry-wide

proceeding convened to address large load cost allocation is exactly the piecemeal treatment that

MDOPC decries in its answer. The coordinated solution MDOPC says is necessary is the Large

Load Order, not a separate complaint that isolates one large load issue from the otherwise

comprehensive discussion.

            Litigation of this Complaint in parallel with considering tariff revisions to address the

Commission’s concerns identified in the Large Load Order would undermine the Commission’s

broader goals. Adjudicating the PJM cost allocation methodology on how it addresses large loads

on a separate record and timeline and with tariff revisions that could conflict with revisions

proposed to address the Large Load Order would create the unwarranted distinctions across

proceedings that the Large Load Order is designed to avoid, and would risk inconsistent outcomes

on interrelated cost-allocation questions.

            B.      MDOPC Fails to Demonstrate Its Replacement Rate Is Just and Reasonable.

           The MDOPC Answer continues to advocate for proposals that are flawed as the PJM TOs

demonstrated in the Motion to Dismiss. The Commission should disregard MDOPC’s replacement

rate proposals because they conflict with Commission policy and rely on impractical and

inappropriate solutions.13

           Regional cost causation relies on the beneficiary principle; costs for transmission upgrades

should be allocated to those who cause them or benefit from them, not merely to the last load to

interconnect.14

           MDOPC’s Answer confirms that its separate large-load track fragments regional planning.

MDOPC argues that PJM will “still run one regional planning process producing one coordinated

plan.”15 But merely packaging final results into a single plan does not alter the fact that, under

MDOPC’s plan, certain system changes (i.e., large loads data centers) would be analyzed apart

from other system changes. Moving away from integrated planning by carving out one specific

type of load would lead to planning inefficiencies. The segmentation MDOPC requests would

“miss opportunities to meet regional transmission needs more cost effectively” because “failing to

engage in holistic regional transmission planning risks failing to identify the most cost-effective

transmission solutions.”16 Inefficiencies also arise because MDOPC’s remedy would impose

fundamental changes to PJM’s planning process.17

                Segmentation would set a precedent for carving others from the planning process, undoing

the progress towards holistic planning. The RTEP, for example, already addresses more than 11

GW of announced generator deactivations, including Brandon Shores in Maryland, through its

integrated process, and Maryland benefits from that holistic treatment.18 For example, PJM

recently sought approval for a “Grid Solutions package” that PJM selected to address multiple

regional reliability violations caused by the deactivation of the 1,272 MW Brandon Shores coal

plant.19 Maryland benefits as it is a net importer of electricity, historically importing about 40%

of its annual electric needs from other states.20 MDOPC offers no principled stopping point to the

planning fragmentation it asks the Commission to authorize.

               C.     MDOPC Improperly Equates Opposition to Its Proposed Remedies with
                      Opposition to Reform.

               MDOPC mischaracterizes the PJM TOs’ reasons for defending the existing cost allocation

methodology by leveling baseless allegations about “perverse incentives.”21 Those allegations

appear to rest largely on the fact that the PJM TOs do not agree with MDOPC’s proposed

alternatives. MDOPC, however, advances untenable alternatives that would return to the flawed

cost allocation methodology that the current cost allocation methodology corrected and that would

fail to meet the unprecedented load growth and speed-to-power demands facing PJM.

               The hybrid cost allocation methodology satisfies cost causation principles.22 MDOPC’s

premise—that concentrated large-load growth outside Maryland has broken the link between costs

and benefits—conflates a factual trend with a rate defect. The PJM TOs do not dispute that load

 is growing but conceding that fact does not render the cost allocation methodology automatically

unjust and unreasonable. The PJM TOs’ will not retread the points raised in the Motion to Dismiss

explaining how the current cost allocation methodology satisfies cost causation principles. It bears

noting, however, that MDOPC’s Answer perfunctorily dismisses the degree of benefits conferred

on Maryland as explained by the PJM TOs. The Complaint must show that the current cost

allocation methodology does not allocate costs roughly commensurate with benefits.23 MDOPC

declares that it “does not need to show that Maryland receives no benefits,” arguing that being

“overcharged” for a benefit violates cost causation.24 But neither the Complaint nor MDOPC’s

Answer establish that Maryland is being “overcharged” in relation to the benefits it receives from

the transmission upgrades.25 Moreover, MDOPC identifies no specific regional baseline project

whose costs were assigned to customers that derived no benefit from it nor any project where the

cost is “grossly disproportionate.”26 Instead, MDOPC asks the Commission to assume that

Maryland is being overcharged for its benefits because load growth is outside of Maryland. But

unsubstantiated assumptions do not carry a complainant’s Section 206 burden.27

           The Complaint also asks the Commission to authorize a major paradigm shift in cost

allocation that the Commission has already recognized as inherently problematic and which is

likely to be mooted by the forthcoming filings in the Commission’s show cause proceeding on

large loads. MDOPC wants the existing cost allocation methodology replaced with a zonal

 allocation that would “allocate the costs of baseline transmission projects driven by large-load

growth to the PJM zone(s) where that load is located, using PJM’s legacy methodology for cost

allocation by geographic area.”28 MDOPC’s solution is a return to a causation-based cost

allocation methodology. Previously, PJM allocated costs under Violations-Based DFAX, which

calculated the contribution of load by zone on the facility that created the need for a transmission

upgrade. The PJM TOs, however, abandoned this causation-based approach due to numerous

problems in assigning costs and because it did not reflect changing system use.29 The PJM TOs

adopted the current cost methodology specifically because the Commission found as unjust and

unreasonable a methodology similar to what the MDOPC now proposes.30 So, far from reflexively

defending the status quo, the PJM TOs seek to avoid returning to a flawed cost allocation

methodology.

III.        CONCLUSION

            For the foregoing reasons, PJM TOs respectfully request that the Commission accept this

answer and ultimately grant its motion to dismiss the Complaint or otherwise deny the Complaint

for the reasons stated herein and in the Motion to Dismiss.
